geometry.rationale: Figure 2 reconstructs more of the figure with actual Three.js primitives—separate 3D plates, slits, arcs, fringe bands, screens, arrows, and point detections—whereas Figure 1 relies heavily on CanvasTexture planes for the detector fringes and particle-dot screens, effectively placing 2D canvases in 3D space. faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful because it reproduces the reference’s 3D perspective layout with an electron source, gray double-slit barrier, expanding golden wavefronts, an interference region, and a black detector screen. concept.rationale: Figure 1 more truthfully represents the core concepts: in panel (a) waves from the source pass through two slits and the two slit-centered wavefronts overlap to make alternating interference bands on a distant detector, matching the requested wave picture (L00012, L00019), and in panel (b) sparse-to-dense dot screens accumulate into the same banded distribution, matching the wave–particle duality idea (L00010, L00014, L00019). Figure 2 also conveys interference and particle buildup, but its barrier and detector screen geometry are much less physically faithful: the plates are broad in the beam direction rather than thin planes at fixed positions, so the slits and detection surfaces are not as clearly or correctly represented as objects electrons pass through and then hit at a distance (L00014, L00019). Figure 2 also tends to hide or reset the particle detections unless the time-lapse is run, weakening the assertion that the three successive screens show sparse, intermediate, and fully resolved accumulated detections (L00014, L00019), whereas Figure 1 shows those stages more directly.

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because it more faithfully matches the rendered textbook-style double-slit scene, with clearer labels, a convincing source-barrier-wavefront-detector layout, and particle buildup/interference behavior that remains visible and responds reliably to controls. Figure 2 has an advantage in using more explicit Three.js geometric primitives rather than textured planes, but it is visually cruder, has less faithful detector/fringe depiction, cramped or invented annotations, and unreliable particle-panel updates that can leave the accumulation screens blank or reset.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better reconstructs the likely textbook geometry: it has four separate narrow glass cylinders on a shared labeled base with correct SAE order, visible pedestal/foot structure, cylindrical oil columns, metal spheres at progressively higher positions for increasing viscosity, and small details such as rims, side outlines, graduation/spout-like lines, and front/top base geometry. Figure 2 also has four cylinders and the correct general ranking, but its proportions are less faithful: the platform is overly massive, the tubes and flared lips are exaggerated, the spheres are very large relative to the tubes, and it omits several structural outline/details that make the source geometry recognizable.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 implements the intended controls more correctly: its drop animation moves all four balls simultaneously with higher SAE grades falling more slowly, its single-tube slider continuously updates the oil color, ball position/drop rate, grade label, and terminal-velocity label across the full 20–50 range, and its label toggle hides/shows reliably using visibility. Figure 2’s interactions are more flawed: the terminal-velocity toggle is effectively broken after being turned on because the label sync loop overwrites display:none, the SAE slider only changes tube 1 while the base label under that tube still says 20, and the drop animation snaps back to a preset snapshot when the fastest ball reaches the floor rather than leaving the animated outcome visible.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more faithful to the reference because it preserves the pale yellow-to-red oil color progression, metallic spherical balls, detailed cylinder rims and bases, and yellow platform with labels in a composition closer to the textbook image. Figure 2 has the same four-cylinder layout, but its base is much darker brown, the balls appear like dark horizontal bands rather than round spheres, and the simplified glassware and muted colors make it less recognizable as the original figure.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 includes the required viscosity labels 20, 30, 40, 50 and the 'Oil viscosity (SAE)' caption in roughly the right locations, and they are marginally more legible than in Figure 2. Figure 2 also has the same labels, but the numbers and caption are extremely tiny and low-readability on the darker base, making them harder to match to the original; both figures add non-original UI text, but Figure 1 better preserves the textbook label content within the diagram itself.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more faithfully teaches the intended relationship: the four grades are ordered 20, 30, 40, 50, the oil colors deepen, and the sphere heights monotonically rise with SAE grade so that greater viscosity corresponds to shorter distance fallen at the same instant (L00012). Figure 2 also shows the qualitative ranking in its default snapshot, but its interactive slider can change tube 1's oil grade/color while the base label still reads 20 and the snapshot sphere height remains the low SAE-20 position, contradicting the idea that sphere position directly encodes the viscosity grade at a fixed time (L00012). Both add quantitative terminal-velocity labels not specified by the brief, but Figure 1's qualitative setup remains internally consistent, whereas Figure 2's controls can create a false displayed relationship between SAE grade, label, and sphere position (L00012).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger across all dimensions: it more closely matches the textbook geometry and rendered appearance with correctly proportioned cylinders, visible rims/base details, metallic spheres, readable SAE labels, and the intended pale-yellow-to-red oil progression. It also implements the interactive behavior more consistently, with simultaneous viscosity-dependent ball drops and a slider that keeps oil color, ball position, grade label, and velocity label aligned, whereas Figure 2 has exaggerated proportions, less legible labels, a darker less faithful base, and controls that can leave the displayed SAE label, oil state, and ball position inconsistent.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better preserves the intended two-panel structure with a standard upward-increasing slope axis, consistent parameter ranges between the sliders and loss plot, and a coherent descent path linked to corresponding fitted lines. Figure 2 has a serious structural error in panel a: the slope axis is effectively inverted, with lower values at the top and higher values at the bottom, and its displayed slope range of -1 to 1 conflicts with the 0 to 4 control range, making the marker and loss-surface layout structurally inconsistent even though its panel b data and line rendering are reasonable.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 keeps the sliders, draggable loss-surface marker, fitted line, and loss readout synchronized across the full advertised parameter ranges, whereas Figure 2 clamps the marker to a much narrower and partly wrong loss-surface domain: intercept values below 0 and slopes above 1 still change the line/readout but leave the marker stuck on the plot edge, so the drawn parameter point no longer represents the actual slider state. Figure 2 also makes dragging unable to reach the advertised slope range up to 4 or negative intercepts, while Figure 1's drag updates both parameters and sliders together over its full surface; Figure 1 has some conceptual scaling issues in the fitted-line slope, but its interactive controls behave much more consistently.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more recognizable as the original: it preserves the two-panel layout, the loss contour panel with the numbered descent path, and the right-panel scatter with multiple teal model lines of increasing slope/intercept. Figure 1 has a more distorted left panel with odd unclipped contour artifacts and a mismatched vertical scale, and its right panel is especially unfaithful because it shows essentially only one nearly horizontal line instead of the family of sloped lines seen in the reference.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has more complete and readable labels matching the original: both panels have clear a)/b) markers, axis titles, the loss title, point labels 0–4, and the line labels 0–4 in panel b. Figure 1’s labels are much smaller, panel b is missing or obscures several of the numbered line annotations, and its panel/axis labels are less legible at inline size; it also includes more distracting explanatory/control text that is not part of the original.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 is conceptually more accurate because it uses the linear model y=φ₀+φ₁x and computes the displayed loss from the shown supervised data as mean squared prediction error, so the link between parameter point, fitted line, and training loss is truthful to the supervised optimization idea (L00007). Figure 1 is worse on that core relationship: its panel-b line uses y=φ₀+0.16φ₁x, so the quantity labeled slope φ₁ is not actually the slope, and its loss is an arbitrary quadratic not the total loss of the displayed data/model, making the two panels only loosely related despite claiming descent and fit behavior (L00007). Both figures violate requested details: Figure 1 gives the intercept axis/range as -1 to 2 instead of 0 to 2, while Figure 2 gives the slope axis as -1 to 1 instead of 0 to 4, and both use brown/orange colormaps rather than the specified teal gradient (L00007). However, Figure 2’s correct model-loss-data relationship outweighs its axis-range error, whereas Figure 1 misrepresents the meaning of the slope parameter itself.

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is stronger overall because it more faithfully matches the reference layout and labeling, and its fitted-line/loss relationship is conceptually closer to the intended supervised optimization model than Figure 1’s scaled slope and arbitrary loss. Figure 1 is better in interactive consistency and parameter-surface geometry, while Figure 2 has a serious slope-axis/domain mismatch that can desynchronize the marker from the sliders; however, Figure 1’s visual unfaithfulness, missing/weak labels, and misleading model-loss relationship make it weaker overall.
